RELIC OF THE PAST.
The remains of a shepherd's hut, near Geelong, Melbourne, built by Von Steiglitz, the first settlers. The chimney is built entirely of granite.

In Mt Alexander Rd, Moonnee Ponds, Victoria is the garbled old trunk of a tree under which Burke and wills (famous Australian explorers) rested on their last trip to the interior. The tree is under the protection of the local municipal council on account of its historical interest.

ON THE WAR PATH. A group ofIFIERS bent on routing out a "rookery" of flying foxes which have been doing great havoc among fruit frees round about Sydney. Despite their formidable appearance they never shot a fox as the creatures had shifted their sleeping quarters overnight.

DEVIL'S GLAW: An extraordinary seed pod which grows in parts of New South Wales and which has been known to kill sheep. The burry portion becomes tangled in the wool on the sheep's cheek and the claws hook underneath the jaw and thus muzzled the sheep, slowly starves to death amidst plenty.

WHEN FLIES ARE BAD. The close up was obtained while this gentleman was forming me of a party of killers who attempted to wipe out a camp of flying foxes which were making disastrous inroads on fruit orchards on the northern confines of Sydney. The creatures fly great distances at night in search of fruit trees but in the daytime seek refuge in more secluded localities where they sleep hanging head down from the limbs of tall trees.

THE GAUNT CLIFF.

This is not a scene along the rugged coast of Scotland, but a cliff at Narrabeen (near Sydney) N.S.W. The castle was built 'by convicts at the time of the settlement of the colony, but now it does duty as a week-end seaside home.

ONCE A REAL FORT.

This charming glimpse of Fort Denison, seen through the trees in the Sydney Botanical Gardens, recalls the days when this little Island was regarded as an adequate protection to Sydney against invasion by sea, and when the ddunteers beneath its tower were used to confine the worst of the convicts in the early settlement.
